messages:
anya_custadmin: Hey team, our Redwood Private agent pods in namespace redwood-agent are CrashLooping on startup. Logs show DNS NXDOMAIN for the control plane hostname and then TLS handshake timeouts. Can you help?

maria_support: sorry you're hitting this — can you paste the agent log lines? short is fine.

anya_custadmin: here are the relevant lines from one pod: 
```
time=\"2025-11-02T16:12:03Z\" level=error msg=\"resolve control plane\" host=\"cp.prod.redwood.internal\" err=\"lookup cp.prod.redwood.internal on 10.96.0.10:53: no such host\"
time=\"2025-11-02T16:12:08Z\" level=warn msg=\"dial tcp 10.20.5.12:443: i/o timeout\" attempt=1
```

raj_se: thanks. that looks like DNS first, then fallback to IP and timed out. do you have any egress-restrictive NetworkPolicies or CNI-level allowlists?

anya_custadmin: we do have a default-deny egress policy across namespaces for compliance. we thought system pods were covered but maybe not.

infra_engineer: quick checks to run: 
1) `kubectl -n kube-system get svc kube-dns -o jsonpath='{.spec.clusterIP}'` -> confirm cluster DNS IP
2) `kubectl -n redwood-agent get pods -o wide` -> see node ips
3) `kubectl -n redwood-agent exec <agent-pod> -- nslookup cp.prod.redwood.internal`

maria_support: also run `kubectl -n redwood-agent get networkpolicy -o wide` to see active policies. If default-deny exists, agent SA or namespace likely needs an explicit egress allow to kube-dns (UDP/TCP 53) and control-plane IPs (TCP 443).

anya_custadmin: ran the nslookup, it fails. `kubectl -n redwood-agent get networkpolicy` returns a default-deny egress rule created org-wide.

raj_se: ok that explains it. two remediation options:
- Short term: add a NetworkPolicy allowing egress from redwood-agent namespace to `kube-dns` service (10.96.0.10:53) and to your control plane CIDR on 443. Example snippet: 
```
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: redwood-agent-egress-allow-dns-cp
  namespace: redwood-agent
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          kubernetes.io/name: kube-dns
    ports:
    - protocol: UDP
      port: 53
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 53
  - to:
    - ipBlock:
        cidr: 10.20.5.0/24   # control plane nodes/ips
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 443
```

- Longer term: add a cluster-scoped exception for system/control-plane egress in your policy generator, or use the operator-managed system-namespace label so infra rules auto-include it.

anya_custadmin: small question: our kube-dns is in kube-system and has no label `kubernetes.io/name=kube-dns`. will that block the policy above?

maria_support: good catch — use a specific `ipBlock` for the cluster DNS IP if there isn't a stable label. e.g. `to: ipBlock: cidr: 10.96.0.10/32` for the DNS service IP.

infra_engineer: also watch for CNI-level host egress allowlists (some CNIs or cloud firewalls only allow node egress to a set of IPs). If you have an egress allowlist at the node or VPC level, ensure control plane IPs and DNS resolver IPs are whitelisted.

raj_se: one more troubleshooting tip: `kubectl -n redwood-agent exec -it <agent-pod> -- curl -v --resolve cp.prod.redwood.internal:443:<control-plane-ip> https://cp.prod.redwood.internal/healthz` will show TLS handshake and SNI behavior.

anya_custadmin: ran the policy change to allow DNS and control-plane CIDR and pods come up! logs show successful TLS handshake. thanks.

redwood-agent-bot: Deploy job #4523: detected agent pod restart; post-deploy healthchecks passed for namespace redwood-agent. :white_check_mark:

maria_support: great — leaving this thread open if you want a followup to harden rules or add automation for system exceptions. :thumbsup:
